Transformations of Anxiety in the Relationship between the Psychotic Child and His Mother

Eleonora Fé d'ostiani

Eleonora Fé d'ostiani

Via Ripense 4/11
00153 Rome
Italy

Eleonora Fé d'ostiani  

Introduction

The reflections put forward in this paper are based on a particular type of experience that I gained during many years of parallel therapeutic work with mothers and their psychotic children. Some of these children were “shell-type”, while others were “entangled”, according to the definitions proposed by Tustin (1981).

Some of the same phenomena turned up time and time again during work with different mothers and children. For example, the child during his session would explicitly and unequivocally act out or symbolize the mother's dreams or deepest anxiety; the mother in turn would refer to the same material later, during her own hour of analysis, and the form was always absolutely superimposed. Or again, several of the child's most tenacious symptoms, which had so far resisted every therapeutic effort, would suddenly disappear at the very moment when I was witnessing the emergence in the mother—or at times in the father—of an archaic fragment of the ego upon which the related experience had been inscribed. Still another example was the incredible capacity these children had to use primary process functioning in order to lend form to physical, mental and emotional states that were latent in their parents.

These and similar occurrences led me to focus attention upon several specific characteristics of these mother-child couples. I was particularly interested in the role played by anxiety in determining and maintaining such a relationship, in which the phenomena I have described, and others like them, prevail over relationships and forms of communication based on language and secondary process generally.

The specific questions which sprung to mind were, “Why such a relationship?” Or, “Why do these relationships all have the same peculiar quality of being dominated by experiences that, as one mother put it, seem ‘Larger than life’?”

This paper does not touch upon cases of childhood psychosis that are a reaction to grossly traumatic elements in the initial holding process, such as a declared psychiatric pathology in one or both of the parents, alcoholism, serious maltreatment of the child, or objective situations within the family that make survival problematic. Such cases require to be dealt with separately. Nor are children considered who present a serious congenital or perinatal organic pathology.

Michael Rustin

Michael Rustin  

This report of action research into the care of young children in day nurseries will be of interest to child psychotherapists, since it is based on the application of psychoanalytic insights to this form of institutional care, and shares the concern of psychotherapists with the quality of relationship between infants and caretakers as its central issue. It makes use of a combination of psychoanalytic and systems theory, and also of Jaques’ and Menzies work on “Social Systems as a Defence against Anxiety” for its organising concepts, and the changes they observed in the day nursery during their work are well analysed using a systems approach.

The research is also an intervention in a wider debate about the desirability or otherwise of the care of young children being undertaken by mothers within the home setting, or through alternative forms of care. The authors are critical of the desirability of providing more day nurseries, the demand for which they attribute to an assorted list of factors, including “the breakdown of the family through divorce or separation … the under-valuation of motherhood, increasing numbers of parents who were themselves in day nurseries or with childminders … the influence of the women's liberation movement and the desire of many women to continue their professional development after childbirth”. They go on to comment that in both “public and some research opinion the stress is on the adult needs with inadequate attention to the child's need. Their own study and psychodynamic findings on child development are cited in support of what they regard as the child-oriented side of this argument. I am by no means sure that they correctly estimate the state of this debate. It is possible to see a number of recent studies of young children and their mothers in various settings as indicating increasing social and academic concern over the quality of life in infancy, both from mothers’ and children's points of view. It is most important in this debate for psychotherapists to insist on the quality of care and relationships needed for the development of young children in whatever setting, and to try to establish some common interest in this, rather than to range themselves against those trying to improve the lives of women.

L.E. Loxterkamp

L.E. Loxterkamp

L.E. Loxterkamp  

Citing numerous intriguing anecdotes Matthews argues convincingly that philosophical wonder and reasoning can be found in young children. A very puzzled John (the author's son, aged 8) asks why, as we have two eyes, we don't see double; and there follows an arresting conversation between father and son that points out some baffling aspects of perception. Tim (aged 6) wants to be certain that everything is not a dream and concludes that everything isn't because “in a dream people wouldn't go around asking if it was a dream”. A girl (9) asserts that there must be a God because he has a name. Ursula (3) inquires where her tummy-pain will go when it goes away. Ian (6), who has to contend with three visiting children choosing to watch a television programme and so preventing him from seeing his favourite, asks his mother indignantly, “Why is it better for three people to be selfish than for one?”

Matthews discusses these examples and many more to show that children, unencumbered by later pressures to conform, naturally experience philosophical perplexity. With elegant conciseness he describes the complex conceptual problems that children articulate and clearly demonstrates that the questions the child poses often differ from the philosopher's only in degrees of sophistication. But, although children lack conceptual maturity, they do exhibit a fresh and genuine puzzlement at the way things are, which indeed is the prime motivation for philosophical reflection—a puzzlement the adult is liable to have left behind. And so Matthews encourages the reader to join the child in thought-experiments, for such intellectual adventures are mutually enjoyable and mutually beneficial.

Now one might believe that this area of philosophical thinking in children has already been well marked out by developmental psychologists and educational theorists. But Matthews asserts that these workers betray a general insensitivity to the child's original grappling with philosophical matters.

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves  

This is a most timely and welcome book. In the dozen years which have passed since his death Winnicott's stock as a theoretician within both Psycho-analysis and child care has if anything increased. Up to the present there has been lacking any simple and systematic presentation of his developmental theory and clinical methodology, but now this volume has filled the gap.

“Systematic” is not perhaps, an epithet which the authors themselves, true to the spirit of Winnicott, would choose to describe their work. For Winnicott in his writings just as much as in his clinical work believed in the constructive value of spontaneous creative activity—the marriage of intellectual discipline and free association. Thus, though his thinking was orderly and directed it never gave the impression of being rehearsed; similarly his papers have a freshness and vigour about them which leave the reader feeling a participant in a journey of discovery, as though the author too whilst writing was all the while feeling his way to his eventual conclusion. Whilst this can be fruitful and exhilarating as a quality in a writer it presents a real challenge for anyone attempting to condense and distil his teachings. To the great credit of the authors of this volume they have succeeded in this difficult task. The book is well planned, being divided into three sections.

[[RunningHead]]

Understanding Children -A Developmental

Marion Burgner

Marion Burgner

12 Kingsley Place
London N6 SEA

Marion Burgner  

I want in this paper to discuss two topics: the first is the Freudian model of normal development; and the second is the use of this developmental model in facilitating our assessment of possible disturbances in childhood within the context of Anna Freud's Diagnostic Profile.

Normal development readily divides itself into phases—oral, anal, phallic, latency, and adolescence, and then -hopefully—sexual and emotional maturity. Phase development was first spelled out by Freud in 1905 in his Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality, in which he wrote of the sexual drives of children. Seventy five years later we are able, with the contributions made by more recent studies in ego psychology, to expand on and delineate what happens to the individual child in each developmental phase: we examine the appropriate expression of sexual and aggressive feelings, the level of relationships to the self and to others, cognitive attainments, the effectiveness or otherwise of the ego defences, the status of the superego within the personality structure, and so on.

Schematically, these developmental phases may be seen in sequence but there is invariably an overlap between each phase and we probably never entirely give up former modes of behaviour—there is some persistence of such modes in later development. For instance, even as adults, we are all familiar with the peremptory demands for need-satisfaction, a mode which originates during the first year of life; but of relevance is the predominance of such behaviour -does it hold sway over our mode of relating or is it simply a minor element within our adult personality structure? As Freud noted in 1933: “Whereas earlier we chiefly emphasised the way in which each of [the developmental phases] passed away before the next, our attention now is directed to the facts that show us how much of each earlier phase persists alongside and behind the later configurations and obtains a permanent representation in the libidinal economy and character of the subject”. A more classical concept in this connection is that of regression, when the individual returns to a former mode of behaviour at a time when the highest level reached is too conflictual or anxiety-provoking. Thus, a child seeking to resolve the complications of, say, his phallic-oedipal relationship may find it altogether too stressful and ambiguous to deal with the fantasy of getting rid of the father whom he simultaneously loves and with whom he identifies, in order to pursue and express his erotic fantasies about mother. Faced with such a dilemma, the boy could regress to the safety of the anal phase where such internal discrepant and threatening demands are held in abeyance and where he can obtain sexualised pleasure from anal rather than phallic expression.

This is a volume in the Fontana series, The Developing Child. The authors are Assistant Professors of Psychology at Harvard University, and authors of Language Acquisition.

At the beginning of the book, the authors set themselves three questions: how does the child learn language so well in such a short time? what is the course of language learning? how do you establish what a child knows? They answer them in reverse order. The first chapter outlines the historical development of language research, some recent testing techniques and basic problems of research. The second, third and fourth chapters outline the course of language development, through sounds, words and simple grammatical rules. The fifth and sixth chapters cover the growing complexity of expression of relationships and concepts.

Anna Freud C.B.E. 1895-1982: An Appreciation

Sandra Ramsden

Sandra Ramsden

Sandra Ramsden  

The death of Anna Freud, aged 86 years, on October 9th 1982, is of great significance in the history of psychoanalysis: it marks the loss of the founder of child psychoanalysis and also the loss of the closest surviving link to her father Sigmund Freud, the founder of psychoanalysis. We have lost that astonishing direct connection to Freud which his daughter gave us, which she indicated clearly sometimes in her rivetting prefaces to comments “my father said …”. Anna Freud's death too was a significant and sad personal moment in history in the lives of many, including many Hampstead Child Therapy Clinic trained child psychotherapists, whose lives would have been so different had the Freuds not moved to London before the war. There are some whose long professional association with Miss Freud spans nearly half a century and for whom her death is a most profound personal loss.

Born in Vienna, the youngest of six children, on December 3rd 1895, Anna Freud's professional life began in education, as a secondary school teacher. Whilst teaching she began a training analysis, published her first paper in 1922 on “Fantasy Life in Children” and in this year became a member of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society. This first paper began a stream of published works. “The Ego and The Mechanisms of Defence” was published in 1936. Her work with her friend and collaborator Dorothy Burlingham produced “Young Children in Wartime” (1942) and “Infants without Families” (1944). “Normality and Pathology” in Childhood was published in 1965. Her recent work was on children and the law written with Solnit and Goldstein and published as “Beyond the Best Interests of the Child” (1979) and “Before the Best Interests of the Child” (1979). Anna Freud's work now in eight volumes, includes many lesser works, some small masterpieces in their simplicity, economy and clarity. All clinicians have their favourites, mine include “On Losing and Being Lost” a brief paper written in 1967 “Certain Types and Stages of Social Maladjustment” another short paper published in 1949.

This book is the result of a consensus conference initiated because of increasing concern at the rapidly escalating rate of caesarian delivery. It is lengthy, 540 pages, but is easy to read, with clearly presented tables and straightforward statistics.

One of the areas covered by the book is an attempt to understand the epidemiology of caesarian birth. The rate trebled in the U.S.A. between 1968 and 1977 but all over the western world the rate of caesarian section is rising steadily although the birth rate is falling. This rise appears to be linked with an increased emphasis on hospital services and technology, because in the Netherlands where the emphasis is on early identification of at risk mothers and conservative management for the remainder, the rate of caesarian section is the lowest (the maternal mortality is lowest and infant mortality is lower than all the other reported countries except Norway).

The book then explores why this escalation has occurred, the problems medical, obstetric and neonatal that have tended to this change in clinical practice. The most important factors appear to be a) Dystocia:—that is problems of unco-ordinate uterine action and/or suspected cephalopelvic disroportion, and b) repeat caesarian because the first delivery was by caesarian section. They are thereby distinguishing between medical emergencies needing a caesarian section, which have remained at much the same level, and a second and increasing group of sections done for less well defined reasons, which of themselves then lead to further caesarian sections.

Of particular interest are the sections on the effects of caesarian birth on the mother, family and infant. As in my own study, there were no gross differences detected in the infants’ behaviour and development as compared with vaginally delivered infants. One of the most striking findings was the greater involvement of fathers where the baby was delivered by caesarian section, the fathers being more responsive to the child, more engaged in caregiving activities, spending more time with the child and expressing more satisfaction with the child's personality. However, the picture was the reverse for the mothers. They had difficulty integrating their labour and delivery experiences, commonly exhibited grieving behaviour and had difficulty focussing on their baby. Those who had had the caesarian under epidural, i.e. were conscious, reported closer feelings than those who had been given a general anaesthetic. Mothers delivered by caesarian section tended to describe themselves as depressed and found it more difficult to cope with negative events such as the child crying or failing to gain weight. There is no comment on the implications for the mother of her sense of failure at being unable to deliver and then mother the child, which the obstetrician (usually male) and father then do so well.

Editorial

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves  

This issue contains two groups of papers each of which are on a particular theme although neither comprises what could properly be called a “symposium”.

On the first group Eileen Orford writes:

“The three papers on Assessment reflect the interest generated by a series of scientific meetings of the Association of Child Psychotherapists which took place in London in 1981 and were devoted to describing work with children and their families preliminary to a decision about treatment … The papers revealed notable differences as well as similarities between the approaches of the Tavistock and Hampstead Clinics. During the ensuing discussions it became clear that there was much interest in the different approaches to and views on this topic. It is with this in mind that the following papers are presented”.

Lisa Miller writes concerning the two papers in honour of Melanie Klein:

“In this year when the centenary of Melanie Klein's birth is being celebrated in many different places it seems appropriate to mark the occasion in the Journal. Rather than to embark on the large task of trying to assess her contribution and importance, now so widely disseminated and recognised, it seems in keeping with her work and aims to publish papers which look further afield, whose emphasis is on future development rather than on consummated achievement. With this in mind we hope to demonstrate in the two papers here presented that the thoughts generated by Melanie Klein's discoveries are still alive and growing “.

By a sad coincidence, plans for the commemorative papers on Melanie Klein were well advanced when news came of the death of Anna Freud, a figure of comparable stature in the history of child psychoanalysis, yet whose views were often sharply at variance with those of Melanie Klein. We begin the issue with a brief tribute to her memory from the pen of the present Chairman of the Association of Child Psychotherapists.

Finally, to round off a number in which reappraisals and commemorations feature so prominently I have included a paper which celebrates another centenary, that of the first recorded treatment in the literature of psychoanalysis, the case of Anna O. I hope my paper helps to show that in history as in childhood, the earliest stages of development are often the most revealing. It also serves as my envoi as Editor. With the new year I hand over responsibility for running the Journal to Lisa Miller, who has been Assistant Editor for the past three years and has played a large part in the preparation of the current issue.

There are rather few studies which look at the adult outcome of adoptions, and Raynor's is valuable for this reason. The book is the result of a study sponsored by the Thomas Coram Foundation for Children. This research attempted to locate all the adoptive families with which the Thomas Coram Foundation had placed a child born between 1948 and 1951 inclusive, and to interview parents and, separately, the adoptees themselves, aged between 22 and 27 at interview. Because the Coram Foundation placements all involved a period of fostering—sometimes for several years—before the adoption, one of the questions Raynor wished to explore was whether this had any effect on outcome. The study therefore included a second group of adoptive families, where the children, born over the same 1948-51 period, had been placed directly for adoption through the National Adoption Society, with no fostering period involved.

Not all the families could be located, or, once located, agreed to the interview. The study finally comprised interviews with 160 families and with 105 of the adoptees. In some cases the adoptees were unavailable for interview for other reasons—e.g. living abroad—but in 36 cases it was the adoptive parents who declined to let their adult son or daughter be interviewed. It appears that frequently their decision reflected fears of stirring up thoughts and feelings about the adoption which parents hoped and believed their child had forgotten about.

Thus already, before we even turn to the interviews themselves, we have an indication of one of the central concerns emerging from the book: the enormous unease generated in some of the parents by discussion of the adoption and the child's separate biological origins.

Raynor approaches the question “How have the adoptions turned out?” by looking at the overall view of the parents and the adoptees, as well as at the current “life-adjustment” of the adoptees. As she points out, the latter criterion is particularly handicapped by the absence of a comparison group of non-adopted people. Without such a group it is difficult to assess whether the 70% “good adjustment” rate is grounds for optimism about adoption outcome, or whether the 30% marginal-to-poor adjustment rate is grounds for pessimism. Perhaps it means more to say that 85% of parents and 80% of adoptees felt their adoption had worked out satisfactorily—usually very much so. It is worth bearing this satisfaction in mind in what follows, because inevitably most of the areas which are of particular interest in the book concern difficulties and dis-satisfactions.

Growing up in Foster Care: One Boy's Struggles

Ann Kaplan

Ann Kaplan

57 Cecile Park
London, N8.

Ann Kaplan  

Introduction

For many children whose parents cannot look after them, foster care offers the only hope for ordinary family life. But there are many barriers in the way of successful family placement, barriers in the foster family, barriers in the child's natural family, and barriers in the child himself. In this paper, I shall focus on one child's difficulties in accommodating to his foster family, as I think his struggles have relevance for our understanding of many children in care.

Many professionals in the field have recognised that understanding and helping children with their feelings is as essential to successful foster home placement as continued support of the foster parents. Dinnage and Kellmer Pringle (1967) state that “the causes of breakdowns (leaving aside for the moment poor selection of, or support for, foster parents) centre around the child's reaction to losing his own family, whether he expresses this by ‘acting out’ or by lack of response”. Flickman (1957) outlines the primary barriers to a child's constructive use of foster family placement, including distrust of people, clinging to old ties, to that which is familiar, and clinging to a hope that his parents will become different. And Thorpe (1980) writes that “time must be devoted to talking with children, both on a factual and emotional level, to help the child to face some of the painful and confusing feelings he is almost bound to have. Failure to help a child to sort out these feelings may result in a child growing up in … ‘an emotional deep freeze!’”

When Mathew began psychoanalytic treatment at age 7½, he faced problems which must be universal to all children in care. He could neither understand nor accept that he would have to spend most of his childhood in foster care. He wanted his own Mother, his own family. And he struggled, against all odds, to maintain a picture of idealised parents who were not to blame for his being in care. It is to the implications of this struggle that I will address myself here. For Mathew's efforts to sustain his picture of idealised parents affected both his emotional development as a whole and his capacity to relate to his foster family.

Some Thoughts on the Question of When to Tell the Child That He is Adopted

Maria Berger , Jill Hodges , Carla Elliott , Sarah Rabb and Frances Salo

Frances Salo

Frances Salo  

The aim of our study1 is to learn about the inner world of the adopted child. Our method consists of examination of analytic material of adopted children treated at the Clinic. This material is contained in weekly reports written by therapists of these children.

So far we have gathered treatment material on 6 adopted children (one in non-intensive treatment). There were 2 boys and 4 girls, their ages at the beginning of treatment ranged from 4½ to adolescence.

In discussing the cases we focussed on issues such as the adopted children's thoughts and fantasies about their adoption and biological parents; the impingement of adoption on their sense of identity, self-representation and self-esteem and the effects of the uncertain sense of identity on their ego and superego development. There was, however, a subject of a more practical nature to which we kept returning. This was the question of when to tell the child that he is adopted.

As the literature on adoption illustrates, this is a controversial topic which has preoccupied professional people concerned with adoption for at least 40 years. In what follows we shall present opinions about the issue of telling prevailing in Great Britain and the USA, and others differing from them. We shall then give an account of our own cases and see what light they throw on the subject.

The views about when the first “telling” should take place fall within a continuum between two opposite positions: 1. The child should be told as early as possible and 2. The child should be told as late as possible, or not at all.

Janis Krohn MSW , Diane Shoemaker MSW and David Klein PHD

David Klein

Ann Arbor
Michigan 48109

David Klein  

Introduction

Anna Freud has often remarked that the body of knowledge compiled by child analysts can provide valuable information and insights for parents, educators, and others concerned with fostering healthy child development. Because psychoanalytic concepts of development are based oh observations of normal children as well as data from treatment settings, they have clear applications to such everyday situations as separations from mother, weaning, toilet training, introduction to group settings, and so on.

The number of infants and young children in day care is expanding, yet concerns about the possible long term consequences of such child care arrangements persist. Research by Spitz (1965), Mahler (1975), Bowlby (1969), Meers (1968), and others has clearly highlighted the need to consider the possible impact on a child's personality development when making any significant changes in the caretaking environment. Some child analysts (Nagera, 1975; Fraiberg, 1977) have also specifically warned that many child care situations, even those which appear superficially adequate or satisfactory, may in fact have a detrimental effect on the child's long term development. Nagera (1975) has argued that full-time day care arrangements, particularly in the earlier pre-school years, can constitute a developmental interference, introducing the risk of distorted object relations, impaired ego development and increased susceptibility to various developmental fixations or arrests.

If we agree that a potential risk to optimal development may be inherent in many day care arrangements, then, given the large number of children being cared for in such arrangements, what can those with a psychoanalytic orientation and with expertise in child development offer? Can we help to minimize any potentially negative impact of the day care solution for child care? In what ways can we help caregivers capitalize on growthenhancing aspects of the day care setting?

The potential risks or benefits of day care for a particular child depend on the interaction of a number of factors. Some of these are unique to the individual, including the child's native endowment and temperament, the nature of past and present attachments to the parents, development of ego abilities and the level of psychosexual development so far reached. Other factors reside in the day care setting itself, such as physical facilities and ambiance, staff-to-child ratio, consistency of staffing, number of hours the child is kept, etc. One crucial variable is the individual caregiver's ability to understand and skilfully handle children.

Growing Points in Psycho-Analysis Inspired by the Work of Melanie Klein

Martha Harris

Martha Harris

8 Broadlands Road
London N6 4AH

Martha Harris  

Mrs. Klein's great discoveries were made possible by her capacity to observe and take an interest in what little children were showing her in their play and conversation. She states categorically that children's play is always meaningful and she certainly approached it with that supposition. Her insights and theoretical formulations were initially inspired and then perhaps somewhat constricted by her devotion to the theories of Freud for whom she had a profound admiration and whose work she saw herself as applying and extending into the field of child analysis. His failure to appreciate her work was indeed a source of continued grief to her. But looking back upon the development of her observations and theories one can see how revolutionary they were, and still are. History tells us how rare it is for one revolutionary to appreciate another who does not stick closely to the party line. To borrow the quotation from Thomas Browne with which Bion prefaces “Learning from Experience” in “Seven Servants” (1977):

“But the mortallest enemy unto knowledge, and that which hath done the greatest execution upon truth, hath been a peremptory adhesion unto Authority, and more especially the establishing of our belief upon the dictates of Antiquity”. (Thomas Browne, “Enquiries into Vulgar and Common Errors: or Adherence unto Antiquity”.)

The writings of Mrs. Klein like those of Freud do indeed court that danger of becoming embalmed in Antiquity: a Talmud or a Koran of Authority if they are used to provide ready answers rather than to stimulate further questions in a field of study, that of the human personality, to whose depth and complexity she has contributed such illumination. It is possible that the extension of the field of child analysis and the continued interest in mother-infant observation which she helped to stimulate in Mrs. Bick, who in turn introduced it into the training of child psychotherapists and analysts, may throw up so many surprises and questions that a tendency to rest complacently in possession of the best of all theories of development will continually be shaken.

Psychotherapeutic Needs of Mothers-To-Be

Joan Raphael-Leff

Joan Raphael-Leff

13 Thurlow Road
London, NW3 5PI.

Joan Raphael-Leff  

Introduction

In a society such as ours, where resources are becoming scarce, the prudent strategies must be: a) early detection of high risk groups and b) preventive measures, thereby reducing the cost of treating established conditions.

Pregnancy offers an ideal opportunity to meet both these requirements. The readiness with which most women apply for professional ante-natal care facilitates early screening for those in need of treatment. Moreover, timely therapeutic intervention during pregnancy can modify the development of a pathological interaction, affecting not only the mother-to-be but her future child. This is particularly true of psychotherapeutic treatment during the ante-natal period. Pregnant women are ideal candidates for brief psychotherapy, being both highly motivated to change before the birth, and by virtue of their pregnancies, being uniquely in touch with their unconscious processes.

Unfortunately, their need for psychotherapeutic treatment is all too often overlooked by the professionals with whom they come into ante-natal contact, and even when detected, the facilities are rarely available for rapid and valid intervention. It is an indictment, that we have focused so much of our attention and resources on the few hours of labour and preparation for these, and given so little thought to the ongoing emotional preparation for motherhood. Indeed, we often tend to forget that the purpose of pregnancy is not merely to create a baby but to produce a mother. A mother is not born with the birth of her child -she is able to mother her newborn only if maternity has been gradually achieved by emotional work accomplished during pregnancy. Most women devote their pregnancy to cultivation and practice of their motherliness; they do so unconsciously, intuitively and creatively, drawing on their concepts of maternal qualities acquired through intimate contact with their own mothers when they were babies and their experience of being mothered and nurtured from infancy on by maternal figures both female and male. Most pregnant women accomplish this psychic task of identification with motherhood and achieve their own unique adaptation to this role, by the time the birth is in sight. However, there are women who cannot accomplish this preparation alone. If the emotional transition to motherhood is to be achieved, they need assistance, preferably in the form of skilled help from a professional psychotherapist.

The Consequences of Severe Early Deprivation as They Emerged in the Psychotherapy of a Girl in Foster Care

Helen High

Helen High

7 Hillside Gardens
London, N6 5SU.

Helen High  

Introduction

This paper sets out to demonstrate the effects of grossly inadequate care during the first three months of life on a little girl's later emotional development.

In describing early infant-mother interaction Wilfred Bion (1962) writes of the importance of the mother's capacity to take in the infant's projections of unbearably distressing emotions, to contain and work them over in her reverie and pass them back to the infant in modified and more manageable form. Bion talks of the infant who has had repeated experiences of this kind of mental containment introjecting the experience of a containing mother and learning progressively to contain himself. Esther Bick has found that the infant who can identify with a mother capable of containing his anxieties in this way, by introjecting that capacity, perceives the containing function in bodily terms as a skin which holds him together. In her paper “The Experience of the Skin in Early ‘Object Relations” (1968) Bick describes examples where lack of such containment in infancy led to disturbances and defects in the experience of the skin as a container and substitute means of engendering the illusion of containment were resorted to. Bick named these secondary attempts at self containment “second skin” phenomena. However, the second skin container does not achieve integration of the personality which is felt to remain in unintegrated bits in danger of falling apart if not continuously held together by these contrived means. This is always a precarious and fragile state.

It seems then that the infant does not start life feeling all of a piece inside his own skin. Normally, the experiences of early empathic containment by the mother, stressed by Bion and Bick as essential for the infant's healthy mental development, would be accompanied by repeated experiences of being picked up and held physically giving rise to tactile sensations in the infant's skin while he was held and handled. I would envisage this as a process in which the bodily sensation of being held is undifferentiated by the baby from the mother's mental and emotional containment so that feeling his skin held and experiencing emotional containment mean one and the same to him and are introjected as one and the same.

This book is a collection of papers by members of the Young People and their Families Workshop at the Tavistock Clinic. The authors come from various professions, social work, psychiatry, child and adult pyschotherapy and psychology. But the way they have worked together to evolve a consistent body of background theory and clinical practice is impressive. Their original professions are indistinguishable in the papers and the book is characterised by a consistency of approach unusual in a collection of twelve papers. At the same time, the book is not monolithic: the authors show that in their clinical work they also have space for their own thinking and to express their own individuality.

The Workshop seems to be a very valuable tool and support to the work being done in the psychotherapy of families by the authors. Christopher Reeves  

Introduction

In the Paper I want to reconsider an episode from the earliest history of psychoanalysis, and in so doing to celebrate a centenary of sorts. Just one hundred years ago this Summer Dr. Josef Breuer concluded the treatment of the twenty three year old Bertha Pappenheim, more familiar under the pseudonym, Anna O. Shortly afterwards, on November 18th 1882, he communicated his findings to his young colleague and protégé, Dr. Freud, and thereby through a chain of consequence the case came to have such a profound influence on subsequent psychoananalytic theory and practice. However, my reason for wishing to re-examine this episode is not simply to record an anniversary, however noteworthy. I hope to show that there is much to merit careful scrutiny about the case itself, and about the reflections Breuer and Freud made upon it in the decade and a half before its publication as the first Case History in their joint Studies on Hysteria (Freud 1895d).

If there is one thing which being a Child Psychotherapist in daily communication with the mental life of small children constantly teaches, it is the realisation of how richly informative a guide can be the way thoughts, feelings and impulses are dealt with in the earliest stages of life for understanding the complexities of adult mental processes. One learns far more about adult mental life from the study of children than about the children's mental life from the study of adults. Similarly with the history of psychoanalysis: to understand current concepts and controversies one must look to the past. Unfortunately, psychoanalysts who have turned to historical research have too often tended to view the past in terms of the present rather than the other way about.

Instead, I propose taking seriously Freud's own dictum in the preface written years later for a new edition of Studies on Hysteria:

“I can give no better advice to anyone interested in the development of catharsis into psychoanalysis than to begin with … (this work) … and thus follow the path I myself have trodden”. (S.E. 2 p. xxxi).

Working towards Interpretation: Early Stages in the Treatment of a “Borderline Psychotic” Boy

John Woods

John Woods

25 Park Avenue South
London N8

John Woods  

The treatment of children with borderline psychotic features* presents particular problems: their object relationships are especially labile; their perception of reality is uncertain and often confused with fantasy; and the ego is easily overwhelmed by anxiety. Interpretation by the therapist is felt as a serious threat to the brittle and shaky defences. Interpretations seem to make the patient worse; he may feel he is being driven mad by them and they may be re-interpreted in concrete terms or in ways quite different from the therapist's intention, or they may be simply not heard. Yet the patient makes a strong demand on the therapist for help and the therapy is valued. Something else is required of the therapist before interpretative work can take place.

In this paper I am attempting a description of a process whereby, during the first eighteen months of treatment, Peter D, a nine-year old boy with borderline psychotic symptoms, became able to embark on the work of analytic psychotherapy. His modes of relating to the therapist and what took place within that relationship were transformed, by stages, to a point where interpretation was possible. The treatment was undertaken in an out-patient clinic, twice a week for the first year and then three times a week, in all for three and a half years. The events of the first eighteen months have provided me with a model for similar pre-interpretative work with borderline children.

Peter's Referral:

Peter was referred at the age of nine and a half by his mother on the advice of his junior school. He was suffering from nightmares and day “horrors”. The family too were suffering from his hyperactivity and provocative behaviour, compulsive whistling, tapping and outbursts of uncontrollable temper; there had been threats to his mother with a knife. At school he was seriously underachieving, unable to read and subject to unaccountable attacks of panic. Their doctor had prescribed Valium but still Peter was hearing chains dragging in the night.

The Conceptual Distinction between Projective Identification (Klein) and Container-Contained (Bion)

Donald Meltzer (Oxford) with Guiliana Milana (Rome) Susanna Maiello (Rome) and Diomire Petrelli (Naples)

Introduction

During seminars in Rome in the Spring of 1982, students of the Rome Course in Child Psychotherapy (related to the Tavistock Clinic, London) presented several cases which Mrs. Harris and I had periodically monitored over the previous three years. Two of them, Mario (G.M.) and Francesco (D.P.) were clearly approaching the termination of therapy, while the third, Antonio (S.M.), a child who had had many autistic features, seemed to be in crisis regarding depressive anxieties and the capacity for thought. Not only were the three boys of similar age (nine years, plus or minus a few months) but also the form of the material was strikingly similar. Resentment of dependence upon a thinking object, hatred of being small and weak, envy of the mother's richness and fertility and jealousy of prospective siblings were all gloriously displayed in the sessions presented to the seminar. But the strategic significance of the material was quite different in the three children and offered a background for the investigation of this important conceptual problem, concerning which there has been much confusion: how do these two concepts, projective identification and container-contained, relate to one another? What are the clinical indicators and how may the distinction be utilised in the clinical situation?

Before describing the clinical material, a brief theoretical preamble may help to focus the problem. In her 1946 paper on schizoid mechanisms, Melanie Klein described the operation of an omnipotent phantasy of intrusion inside the body and mind of another (external) person, producing a form of narcissistic identification and a corresponding alienation from one's true identity. Work in the following years by her followers traced a wide range of pathological phenomena to this mechanism, including claustrophobia, agoraphobia, hypochondria, manic-depressive states, disturbances of thought and judgment, certain psychotic confusional states; as well as demonstrating that the mechanism operated also with internal objects and had a specific connection with certain types of masturbation, anal in particular. Disturbances in character development variously known as pseudo-maturity and false-self seemed also to be a consequence of its wide employment.

Letter to the Editor

Dear Sir,

We are grateful for the opportunity of replying to the recent Review* of our Research Report on day nursery care to the Department of Health and Social Security. While Michael Rustin in many ways appeared to find the Report valuable e.g. “insightful and informative”, “valuable changes”, “useful implications”, “account fundamentally right”, at the same time he makes a number of criticisms of the Report which badly misrepresent the focus of the research, the stance and professional views of the authors and the research methodology. He also omits to discuss the recommendations concerning the development of day nurseries as therapeutic and educational institutions. We wish to take up some of Rustin's comments in detail.

Rustin writes: “They hypothesize that children in the care of such a nursery (where the project was based) will be unlikely to develop satisfactorily, and may well deteriorate, and seek to test this view” (p. 90). We actually did not set out to do this (although a minor focus of the Report provides some additional evidence that this is the case1). The main thrust of the action research was not to prove day nurseries put at risk the psychological and social development of children, particularly the under 3′s. This was assumed as a starting point on the basis of research2 for the D.H.S.S. carried out by a Tavistock team led by Isabel Menzies in 1970/71. The main thrust of the action research was, given this, to see how far it was possible to go in improving the level of care in an ordinary local authority day nursery (within the limitations of the system and resources available).

Finding a Way to the Child

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin

Belsize Lane
London NW3

Margaret Rustin  

I am going to describe some assessment work with the only child, a six year old boy, of a divorced mother.

They had been referred to the clinic by their GP who was asking for psychotherapy for mother, which had previously been recommended at another clinic, and indicating that the child's state of mind and health gave considerable cause for concern.

Mrs. S. had consulted her GP about her persistent headaches and leg pains, and about Alex's hair, which was falling out. Hospital investigations suggested that all their symptoms were fundamentally psychosomatic and not organic. Some months later, mother again expressed worry about Alex, who was speaking of “wanting to die”, saying that he would use a knife, and also sleepwalking. His mother felt he was disturbed by his frequent visits to his father—agreed access was three times weekly.

When this case was first considered, we thought it likely that both mother and son might need individual therapy. The degree of somatisation was worrying, but mother's persistent search for help was also striking. We felt concerned to provide a framework in our initial contact which could help her to distinguish between her personal needs and those of Alex—we had to devise an approach which took account both of her own difficulty and of her parental worry and active concern about Alex.

We decided to offer her an exploratory consultation with a social worker to sort out whether she wanted assessment for Alex, whether a treatment might be feasible practically, and to clarify the legal situation vis-a-vis care and control of the boy. A consultation took place in which it was explained to her that a therapist could be available for her subsequent to an assessment of Alex, and that a decision would be taken jointly with her about what help would be appropriate for him. Our initial work was therefore designed to try to clarify whether there was available a parental framework of responsible concern which would provide a reliable setting for work with the child. Mrs. S. accepted this approach and kept to the appointments arranged, which involved a longish gap between exploration with her and assessment of Alex because of the summer holiday period.

W.R. Bion: The Long Weekend. Fleetwood Press, 1982 £9.00.

T.P.S. Miller

T.P.S. Miller

T.P.S. Miller  

Anyone who has read “Goodbye to All That” or “Memoirs of an Infantry Officer” will know how lightness of touch and deftness of language in describing the horror of the Western Front can hint at a worse horror, something unimaginable, unspeakable. “The Long Weekend” has the same quality. But it has an added element which focusses that horror into the cramped confines of an ungainly steel lozenge: the secret weapon, the battlefield monster, the tank. Bion was one of the earliest tank officers. His account of tank warfare gives “The Long Weekend” value as an historical source which Graves's and Sassoon's more self-consciously literary works somehow miss.

Bion sought out the tanks because they were secret. The first he saw at Bovington was larger than life: “A metallic hammering came from inside; a soldier got out and the day came to life again”. The machines came to dominate those who served them. Where other junior officers were concerned with their men, tank officers had to be concerned with their machines. They would lay white tapes to guide these short-sighted monsters into battle; walk in front probing the ground for softness with an ash-plant; perform prodigies of heroism in trying to rescue them from the mud of no-man's-land. Tanks had names, and sex. Those with 6 pounder guns were Males; those with just machine guns, Females. The original prototype, Little Willie, fathered a line which began with Mother, a Mark I Male. Given his later career, Bion's refusal to tangle with this curiously confused sexual symbolism is a mark of his exemplary control. He himself served exclusively in Male tanks.

Like every tank officer, Bion had to risk men to save his machine. When he reached the front in 1917 his first action was an attack on a strong point on the Passchendaele battle front. The tank ditched in the mud. After fending off the questions of the intelligence officer, Clough Williams-Ellis (who later built the fantasy village of Portmeirion), about the point at which the alluvial mud became cretaceous, Bion and his crew set out to fetch back their tank. But if was lost amid the exploding shells.

Assessment for Psychotherapy

Isca Wittenberg

Isca Wittenberg

Belsize Lane
London NW3

Isca Wittenberg  

Introduction

Assessment is a big subject. To arrive at something we might appropriately call diagnosis we need to do far more than what I wish to discuss in this paper. We would have to take into consideration the following areas of the spectrum:

the picture of the world the patient has in mind, i.e. the kind of internal world he has come to have as a result of his experiences. These experiences will be the result of the interaction between his impulses, the phantasies arising from them on the one hand, and, on the other, the external factors of his life, particularly the quality of the nurturing care he has received.

the home environment—external factors of the family as well as the organisation of his parents’ internal world, e.g. what was the position of the child in the family, was mother depressed in the child's infancy; was father violent; the relationship between the parents; the nature of their attitude to the patient.

external world—the society he lives in and the influence this exerts on him and his family, for instance, do they live in a delinquent sub-culture, is the adolescence exposed to drugs, and so on.

It will be seen that this is an interactional model, namely, development is seen as based on the interaction between internal and external factors*.

Internal factors are the child's endowment, especially the inborn relative strength of the capacity for love vis-a-vis his hate. If the infant has a low tolerance of frustration and is easily angered, this means that he will be more easily subject to intense and frequent persecutory anxieties. These in turn may make it difficult for him to accept help when it is forthcoming. A more favourably endowed infant will put up better with frustration and can be more easily consoled after an upsetting experience, thus reestablishing a loving contact more rapidly. External factors comprise the actual outer events in his life and also the amount and quality of the nurturing he has received, e.g. the understanding of the meaning of his behaviour and feelings which could help him to sort out his experience and lessen his anxiety. In terms of assessment, let us take two extremes. A child who comes from a relatively sane and stable background with no major traumas in his life but presents as severely disturbed is quite likely to have a high degree of destructiveness or envy in his make-up and might therefore be a difficult and a long term treatment proposition.
